what_its_for: Mitotane is used to treat a type of cancer called adrenocortical carcinoma, which is cancer of the adrenal gland. It works by damaging the cancer cells in the adrenal gland and lowering the amount of certain hormones your body makes. Your doctor may use it when the cancer cannot be removed by surgery or has come back after surgery.
how_to_take: Take mitotane by mouth with food. Eating food with this medicine helps your body absorb it better and may reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablets whole. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level of the medicine in your body. Do not crush or break the tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you it is safe to do so.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how well you tolerate the medicine and how your body responds. A typical starting dose is 2 to 6 grams per day, divided into 3 or 4 smaller doses taken throughout the day. Your doctor may increase your dose up to 9 to 10 grams per day or higher. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribes. Your blood levels of mitotane will be checked regularly to make sure you are getting the right amount.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time for your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store mitotane at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C and 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet. Ask your pharmacist about the safest way to dispose of any medicine you no longer need.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking mitotane, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can cause serious drowsiness, confusion, and dizziness. Avoid taking sedatives, sleeping pills, or anti-anxiety medicines without talking to your doctor first, as these can make the drowsiness worse. Women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets — and even caregivers should use gloves when handling this medicine. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell all your doctors and dentist that you are taking mitotane before any procedures or surgeries.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that will not stop; unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme tiredness or weakness; severe dizziness or confusion; trouble walking or loss of balance; vision changes; signs of low cortisol (adrenal crisis) such as sudden severe weakness, dizziness, fainting, or severe stomach pain — this is a medical emergency; skin rash or signs of an allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat; dark urine or yellowing of the skin or eyes; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. Also call your doctor before stopping this medicine, as it should not be stopped suddenly without medical guidance.
when_it_works: Mitotane works slowly. It may take several weeks to months before you and your doctor can tell if the medicine is helping. Blood and urine tests, as well as imaging scans, will be used to check how well the treatment is working. Do not stop taking mitotane just because you do not feel immediate changes — continue taking it exactly as prescribed and keep all your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Mitotane can seriously harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Women who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for a period of time after stopping — ask your doctor how long. Do not breastfeed while taking mitotane, as the drug may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to the side effects of mitotane, especially dizziness and confusion. Use with extra caution. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine and your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Steroid supplementation: Because mitotane lowers your body's natural cortisol levels, your doctor may prescribe steroid replacement medicines. It is very important to take these as directed and to carry a medical alert card or bracelet indicating you are on mitotane therapy in case of emergency.
